How to Analyse Your Web Reputation: A Step-by-Step Audit

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

A useful online reputation analysis is a structured audit, not a quick look at Google. It maps what appears for your branded searches, reviews the platforms where customers judge you, checks autocomplete, social channels and AI answers, scores the sentiment of each element by its visibility, and ends with a short, prioritised list of actions.

What an online reputation analysis should cover

The audit should reproduce what a real customer, partner or investor sees when they look you up, and nothing less. That means six layers: branded search results, review platforms, search suggestions and images, social networks and forums, answers from AI assistants, and the overall sentiment that emerges from them.

Each layer is examined separately and then combined into a single picture. The same method works for a company, a professional practice or an individual, whether the audience is local, as for a clinic in Bologna, or national, as for a brand selling across Italy. What changes is the list of queries and platforms, not the logic. Repeat the analysis at regular intervals, because a reputation audit is a snapshot and its value grows when you can compare it with the previous one.

Branded searches and the page-one map

Start by listing the queries that matter: the brand or person's name alone, the name with the city, with the main product, with words like “recensioni”, “opinioni” or “truffa”, and the names of key executives. Run each search on google.it in a private window, both on desktop and on mobile, with the location set to the markets you serve.

For every result on page one, and ideally page two, record the URL, position, type of source and tone. A simple classification makes the map readable:

TypeExamplesControl
OwnedWebsite, blog, official social profilesFull
ManagedGoogle Business Profile, directory listings, marketplace pagesPartial
EarnedPress articles, interviews, partner pagesIndirect
Third partyReview sites, forums, complaint portals, news archivesNone

The map quickly shows the real problem. A page one with three owned results, five managed ones and a single negative article is a very different case from a page one where owned assets are missing and unknown websites define the brand.

Reviews: rating, volume and patterns

Review platforms are often the most influential layer, because they appear directly in Google Maps and in the local panel. Audit every platform relevant to your sector: Google Business Profile for almost everyone, TripAdvisor and Booking for hospitality, Trustpilot for e-commerce, specialised portals for healthcare or legal services.

For each platform record the indicators that buyers notice:

  • average rating and total number of reviews;
  • recency, meaning how many reviews arrived in the last three and twelve months;
  • share of reviews with a reply from the business and the tone of those replies;
  • recurring themes in negative reviews, such as delays, staff, prices or after-sales service;
  • reviews that may breach platform policies, such as fake, off-topic or conflict-of-interest posts.

The themes are the most valuable output. They separate operational issues that need fixing inside the company from isolated or suspicious reviews that may qualify for reporting.

Autocomplete, images, social channels and AI answers

Search suggestions shape perception before anyone clicks. Type the name slowly in Google and note every suggestion and every “related search” at the bottom of the page; terms such as “scam” or “complaints” next to a brand name deserve immediate attention, as we explained in our article on negative Google suggestions. Google Images is checked the same way, looking for outdated logos, unflattering photos or images taken from unrelated people with the same name.

Social channels and forums complete the picture: mentions on Facebook groups, Instagram, LinkedIn, Reddit and Italian consumer forums, plus the activity and responsiveness of your own profiles. Finally, ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews who you are and whether you are reliable. Their answers summarise the sources above and often reveal which pages carry most weight. Our guide to AI Overviews and generative search explains why this layer can no longer be skipped.

Scoring sentiment so results can be compared

Sentiment becomes useful only when it is scored consistently. Assign each element a value on a simple scale, for example from minus two for clearly harmful to plus two for clearly positive, and weight it by visibility: a negative article in position two matters much more than one at the bottom of page two.

The weighted total gives a single number for each query and layer, which you can track over time. Keep the scoring rules written down so that the next web reputation analysis, perhaps carried out by another person, produces comparable results. Add short notes explaining every negative score, because the reason behind a number is what turns it into an action.

A reputation audit is only as good as its comparability. Same queries, same scoring rules, same platforms, every time.

Prioritising actions after the audit

The analysis should end with a short list of actions ranked by impact and feasibility, not with a long report. The most visible problems that can be solved quickly come first; slow, uncertain actions are planned but do not block the rest.

In practice, actions fall into four groups:

  1. quick fixes, such as correcting outdated information on owned and managed profiles and replying to unanswered reviews;
  2. removal candidates, meaning content that may breach the law or platform policies, such as fake reviews, defamatory posts under art. 595 c.p. or personal data that can be erased under GDPR art. 17;
  3. operational issues, the recurring complaints that only the business itself can solve;
  4. building work, new content and profiles that strengthen page one over time.

Each action needs an owner and a deadline, and the next audit verifies the result.
